title: Integral split root datum and geometric-fibre lattice criteria
statement:
An integral group scheme means a group object over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$, using the group diagrams of [def-sc-group-scheme] over this base [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. A reductive integral group scheme is smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], affine [pqf-def-affine-morphism], finitely presented [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation], with connected geometric fibres [def-weil-connected-scheme] and no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup in any geometric fibre. Unipotent means that in a faithful matrix representation all geometric points are unipotent matrices, so $(u-I)^N=0$ for some $N\geq1$. A split maximal torus is a closed subgroup [def-weil-closed-immersion] $U\simeq D_{\mathbf Z}(M)$ with fibrewise maximal tori, for a finite-rank free abelian group $M$; $D_A(M)=\operatorname{Spec}A[M]$ has the Hopf operations of [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group]. Characters and cocharacters are homomorphisms to and from $\mathbf G_m$, paired by $\chi\circ\lambda(t)=t^{\langle\chi,\lambda\rangle}$. A reduced root datum $(M,\Phi,M^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ consists of a finite-rank free abelian group $M$, its integer dual $M^\vee$, finite subsets $\Phi\subset M\setminus\{0\}$ and $\Phi^\vee\subset M^\vee\setminus\{0\}$ in bijection $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee$, with $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$. The reflections $s_\alpha(m)=m-\langle m,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ and their duals permute the roots and coroots compatibly, the group generated by the reflections is finite, and $\mathbf Q\alpha\cap\Phi=\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$. Let $G$ be a reductive integral group scheme with a specified split maximal torus $U=D_{\mathbf Z}(M)$. There is a reduced root datum $(M,\Phi,M^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ whose base change identifies with the group root datum of $(G_k,U_k)$ for every algebraically closed field $k$ with $\mathbf Z\to k$. Here roots mean the nonzero characters of the full $U$-coaction on the tangent module $\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ at the identity, and coroots are the corresponding homomorphisms $\mathbf G_m\to U$ in the geometric group root datum. These roots have constant support $\Phi$ and their weight modules over $\mathbf Z$ are free of rank one. The same root and coroot identifications hold for the base-changed split group over every nonzero commutative ring $A$ and every geometric fibre over $A$. The geometric fibres of $G$ are semisimple if and only if $\Phi$ spans $M\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$. In that case put
$$P=\{v\in M\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q:\langle v,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\mathbf Z\text{ for all }\alpha\in\Phi\}.$$
The geometric fibres are simply connected if and only if $M=P$. Semisimple means having no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup, where solvable means that iterated commutator subgroups become trivial. Simply connected means that every surjective homomorphism onto the geometric fibre from a connected semisimple group with finite central scheme-theoretic kernel is an isomorphism. The empty root set and the zero lattice are allowed.

source.place: Definition 5.1.1 and Example 5.1.4, printed pp.136-137; Proposition 5.1.6 and Example 5.1.7, pp.138-139; Exercise 1.6.13(ii) and the introductory paragraph of Exercise 6.5.2, p.235. Read online; WANTED locally as literature/conrad-reductive-group-schemes.pdf. No Stacks tag states this reductive-group structural theorem.

proof.text: Choose a basis of the given finite free lattice $M$, so $U=D_{\mathbf Z}(M)$ is $\mathbf G_m^r$. By [lem-sfb-relative-diagonalizable-character-duality], characters and cocharacters of this torus are locally integer homomorphisms $\mathbf Z\to M$ and $M\to\mathbf Z$, respectively. Every nonempty open of $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$ contains $(0)$, so locally constant integer homomorphisms are constant. Thus the specified character and cocharacter lattices are exactly $M$ and $M^\vee$, with the evaluation pairing: composing their Hopf maps sends $t$ to $t^{\lambda(m)}$. The Hopf operations in [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group] also show directly that $(D_{\mathbf Z}(M))_A=D_A(M)$ for every ring $A$.

Apply [lem-sfb-relative-tangent-weight-base-change] over the nonzero Noetherian ring $\mathbf Z$ to the conjugation action of $U$ on $G$. It gives a finite projective tangent module $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_m\mathfrak g_m$, with finite support and weight summands commuting with every ring base change. The simultaneous local constancy of the weight ranks in [lem-sfb-relative-torus-bundle-weights] makes each rank constant on $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$, by the generic-point argument of step 1. In the geometric generic fibre [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections] says that every nonzero weight has dimension one. Let $\Phi$ be those nonzero weights. A finite projective $\mathbf Z$-module embeds as a direct summand of a finite free module, so [lem-weil-subgroup-finite-free-abelian-group-free] makes every $\mathfrak g_m$ free. Its rank is its generic-fibre dimension; hence $\mathfrak g_m$ has rank one for $m\in\Phi$ and is zero for every other nonzero $m$. Weight base change now identifies $\Phi$ with the roots of every geometric fibre, in every characteristic.

source.place: Example 5.1.4, printed p.137; Section 4 opening weight decomposition

proof.text: For each $\alpha\in\Phi$ also $-\alpha\in\Phi$, by the clause $\mathbf Q\alpha\cap\Phi=\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$ of [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections] in the geometric generic fibre, so by step 2 the two opposite root modules $\mathfrak g_{\pm\alpha}$ are free of rank one. Use [lem-sfb-relative-canonical-root-exponential] to obtain their canonical root subgroup maps, then [lem-sfb-relative-opposite-root-reflection-map] to obtain $\alpha^\vee:\mathbf G_{m,\mathbf Z}\to U$. That statement identifies its geometric fibres with the usual coroots and makes the construction commute with arbitrary base change. By [lem-sfb-relative-diagonalizable-character-duality] and connectedness as in step 1, this homomorphism is a single element of $M^\vee$, not a choice depending on the fibre. Put $\Phi^\vee=\{\alpha^\vee:\alpha\in\Phi\}$. The equality $\chi_\alpha(\alpha^\vee(c))=c^2$ gives the integer identity $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$.

source.place: Definition 5.1.1 and the paragraph following it; Theorem 4.2.6, applied in each rank-one centralizer

proof.text: Evaluate these lattice elements in the geometric generic fibre. Choose a Borel pair by [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]; conjugate its maximal torus to the specified $U_{\overline{\mathbf Q}}$ using [lem-sfb-borel-maximal-torus-conjugacy], and conjugate the Borel by the same element. The root-datum assertion of [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure] now applies to this pair. [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections] gives the reflection formula, finite Weyl group, compatibility of conjugation with coroots, one-dimensional root spaces, and reducedness. The torus character and cocharacter identifications of step 1 are identifications of integer lattices, so each of these equalities is the very same equality in $M$ or $M^\vee$. In particular the root-coroot assignment is bijective, its dual reflections permute the coroots compatibly with the root permutations, and the reflection group is a subgroup of the finite geometric Weyl group. This proves every root-datum axiom in the statement. For any nonzero ring $A$, the tangent comparison of [lem-sfb-relative-tangent-weight-base-change] identifies the nonzero weight modules with $A\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathfrak g_\alpha\simeq A$. The arbitrary-base-change clause of [lem-sfb-relative-opposite-root-reflection-map] identifies the coroots with the base changes of the same integer cocharacters. Thus the claimed root and coroot identifications hold over $A$ and over each of its geometric fibres, including for nonreduced or disconnected $A$.

source.place: Proposition 5.1.6 and its proof, printed p.138; base-change compatibility from Theorem 4.2.6

proof.text: For any algebraically closed $\mathbf Z$-field $k$, the torus $U_k$ is a split maximal torus of the reductive group $G_k$ by hypothesis. Apply [lem-sfb-semisimple-roots-span] with its actual character lattice $M$ and the root set $\Phi$ identified above. It says precisely that $G_k$ is semisimple if and only if $\Phi$ spans $M\otimes\mathbf Q$. The right-hand condition is independent of $k$, proving the asserted equivalence for all geometric fibres at once.

source.place: Proposition 21.48, printed p.439; compare Conrad Example 5.1.7, p.138

proof.text: Assume the span condition of step 5. If the geometric fibres are simply connected, fix any one, for example over $\overline{\mathbf Q}$. Choose a Borel pair by [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure] and conjugate it to put its torus at the specified one, using [lem-sfb-borel-maximal-torus-conjugacy] as in step 4. The group is semisimple by step 5 and simply connected by assumption, so [lem-sfb-simply-connected-character-lattice] identifies its actual character lattice with the elements pairing integrally with all coroots. Under steps 1--4 that equality is exactly $M=P$. No claim about the characteristic-zero Lie algebra is used.

source.place: Proposition 23.59 and paragraphs 22.8--22.11; compare Conrad Exercise 1.6.13(ii)

proof.text: Conversely assume $M=P$, fix an algebraically closed $\mathbf Z$-field $k$, and take an arbitrary surjective homomorphism $f:H\to G_k$ from a connected semisimple group with finite central scheme-theoretic kernel. A semisimple group is reductive by [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Apply [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization] to write $f$ as a faithfully flat map onto a closed subgroup $I\subseteq G_k$. Surjectivity makes the defining ideal of $I$ vanish at all points of $G_k$. The scheme $G_k$ is reduced by [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced]; hence this ideal lies in its zero nilradical, so $I=G_k$ and $f$ is faithfully flat. Choose a Borel pair using [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure] and conjugate it to $(B,U_k)$ by [lem-sfb-borel-maximal-torus-conjugacy], as in step 4. By [lem-sfb-central-isogeny-borel-root-compatibility] it lifts to $(B_H,T_H)$, with roots identified by pullback and coroot pairings preserved. By [lem-sfb-isogeny-root-power-laws], $u=f_T^*:M\hookrightarrow X^*(T_H)=M_H$ has finite cokernel. The central-kernel hypothesis forces every root exponent in that statement to equal one, even when the kernel is nonreduced.

source.place: Proposition 23.29, printed p.493 (central isogeny reduction); Theorem 5.39, p.108; Propositions 23.5--23.6

proof.text: Identify $M_H\otimes\mathbf Q$ with $M\otimes\mathbf Q$ by $u_{\mathbf Q}$. For $x\in M_H$ put $v=u_{\mathbf Q}^{-1}(x)$. The coroot-pairing equality in [lem-sfb-central-isogeny-borel-root-compatibility], extended rationally, gives $\langle v,\alpha^\vee\rangle=\langle x,\alpha_H^\vee\rangle\in\mathbf Z$ for every root $\alpha$. Thus $v\in P=M$. It follows that $x=u(v)$, proving that $u$ is surjective as well as injective. The isomorphism criterion in [lem-sfb-root-datum-isogeny-realization] now applies to this very isogeny: all its root exponents are one by step 7 and $u$ is an isomorphism. Hence $f$ is an isomorphism. Since $f$ was arbitrary this proves that $G_k$ is simply connected, and since $k$ was arbitrary it proves the remaining equivalence for all geometric fibres.

source.place: Proposition 23.29, printed p.493, displayed lattice inclusions and final sentence

proof.text: The arguments permit $\Phi=\varnothing$: the root and coroot constructions are empty, and the span condition is then exactly $M=0$. In that case $P=\{0\}$; the same central-isogeny argument applies in rank zero. If $M\ne0$ and $\Phi=\varnothing$, the semisimplicity condition fails, so no weight-lattice condition is asserted. Nonzero base rings are retained, ensuring the base change of a rank-one root module remains nonzero.
